# Strict cap certificates and parity geometry

Throughout this note d>=1, S=C intersect (Z^n x R^d) has positive mixed
volume, and mu is that volume normalized to one. Write F=max_{y in S}
depth_mu(y), and suppose F<alpha<1. The conclusions below hold for any such
alpha; the intended application is alpha=2^{-n} gamma_d.

## Removing zero-volume fibers preserves the optimization

Let P be the finite set of integer coordinates with positive-volume fibers.
It is nonempty. Every point of conv(P) has a full-dimensional C-fiber: write
it as a convex combination of points of P and use convexity of C and the
fact that a Minkowski combination with a positive coefficient of a
full-dimensional body is full-dimensional. Consequently

  P = conv(P) intersect Z^n.

Every nonempty zero-volume fiber has integer coordinate outside conv(P).
Strict separation of that point from the compact convex set conv(P) gives
a vertical closed halfspace containing the whole zero-volume fiber and no
positive-volume fiber. All points of such a fiber therefore have depth zero.
Thus the optimization can be restricted to

  S_plus = [C intersect (conv(P) x R^d)] intersect (Z^n x R^d),

which is compact, has exactly the fibers indexed by P, and has the same
probability measure. Its inducing convex set need not be full-dimensional;
that causes no problem for the mixed-integer Helly theorem.

## Strict equal-mass cap certificate

There exist m<=2^n(d+1), a common number tau<alpha, and closed caps
H_i={w:a_i dot w>=b_i}, i=1,...,m, with the following properties:

1. Every continuous normal component v_i of a_i=(u_i,v_i) is nonzero.
2. mu(H_i)=tau for all i.
3. The open interiors U_i={w:a_i dot w>b_i} cover S_plus.
4. For every i there is p_i=(z_i,x_i) with x_i in int(C_{z_i}) such that
   a_i dot p_i>b_i and a_j dot p_i<b_j for every j!=i.
   In particular, the exclusive portion of cap i contains a positive-volume
   ball in fiber z_i.

Proof. Choose F<alpha_0<alpha. Every y in S_plus belongs to some closed
halfspace of mass less than alpha_0. Move its boundary outward slightly;
continuity of measure from above ensures its mass remains below alpha_0,
and y now lies strictly inside. Perturb its normal to make its continuous
component nonzero. Because S_plus is bounded and y has a strict interior
margin, a sufficiently small perturbation preserves the interior condition
and puts the perturbed cap inside a slightly enlarged original cap of mass
less than alpha_0. Compactness gives a finite open cover by such caps.

For a fixed nonvertical normal, all hyperplane boundaries have zero mu-mass.
Its cap-mass function f(b)=mu({a dot w>=b}) is continuous and takes every
value between zero and one. Enlarge each cap to have mass alpha_0. Among
thresholds giving mass alpha_0, choose the smallest threshold, so the chosen
cap is the largest cap of this mass. These closed caps still cover S_plus.
Take an inclusion-minimal closed subcover.

The mixed-integer Helly theorem, h(Z^n x R^d)=2^n(d+1), bounds its size by
h. Indeed the complements are open convex halfspaces; together with the
convex inducing set they have empty mixed-integer intersection. Helly gives
a subfamily of at most h sets, and minimality of the cap cover forces every
selected cap into that subfamily. The open-set version of finite Helly
follows from the closed-set version: if all h-subfamilies were feasible,
choose their finitely many witnesses and shrink each open halfspace slightly
to a closed halfspace retaining all relevant witnesses. The full family
remains infeasible, a contradiction.

For each cap i, minimality gives a witness in S_plus lying outside all other
closed caps, with strict inequalities there. In its full-dimensional fiber,
perturb the witness into the interior while preserving those inequalities.
A small neighborhood remains outside all other caps and must therefore be
covered by cap i. Since its continuous normal is nonzero, a point of this
neighborhood lies strictly inside cap i. This gives the desired strict
witness for the present cover.

Finally increase the common cap mass from alpha_0 to tau>alpha_0, choosing
tau<alpha sufficiently close to alpha_0. The smallest threshold realizing
tau tends to the previously chosen smallest threshold as tau decreases to
alpha_0. To see this, monotonicity gives a one-sided limit; continuity of f
makes that limit a threshold of mass alpha_0, and its being no greater than
the smallest such threshold forces equality. Thus the enlargement can be
made sufficiently small to keep every witness strictly outside every other
cap. Every new threshold is strictly smaller than its previous value, so
the new open caps cover every point of the former closed cover. They have
common mass tau<alpha, and retain the strict interior witnesses. QED.

## Explicit inequalities forced by parity

For the certificate above put

  r_i = a_i dot p_i-b_i > 0,
  s_ij = b_i-a_i dot p_j > 0  (i!=j).

If z_i and z_j have the same coordinatewise parity, their midpoint belongs
to S_plus. It is strictly outside every cap k other than i,j. The open cover
therefore gives

  r_i > s_ij  or  r_j > s_ji.                         (P)

Equivalently, the normalized matrix t_ij=s_ij/r_i has, on each same-parity
pair, at least one directed entry strictly below one. This does not assert
that both entries are below one or that their product is below one.

More generally, if lambda_i>=0, sum lambda_i=1, and sum lambda_i z_i is
integer, then convexity and the cover imply

  max_i [r_i lambda_i - sum_{j!=i} s_ij lambda_j] > 0. (B)

Thus the polytope of barycentric weights satisfying all the reverse weak
inequalities has integer-free image under lambda -> sum lambda_i z_i.
These are exact finite-dimensional consequences, not a volume estimate.

## Quantitative volume promotion at a distinct midpoint fiber

Fix two indices i,j whose witness integer coordinates are distinct and have
the same parity. Let A_i subset C_{z_i} and A_j subset C_{z_j} be compact
convex positive-volume subsets of the respective strict exclusive regions.
Write V_i=vol_d(A_i), V_j=vol_d(A_j), and M=H_d(S). Then

  2 tau M >= V_i+V_j+
      ((V_i^(1/d)+V_j^(1/d))/2)^d.                 (V)

Proof. Their Minkowski midpoint B=(A_i+A_j)/2 belongs to the fiber at
(z_i+z_j)/2. Every point of B is strictly outside every cap other than i,j,
so B is covered by U_i union U_j. Since its integer coordinate differs from
both endpoint coordinates, its volume is separate from those of A_i and
A_j in the fiber sum. The latter two sets contribute only to their own caps.
Therefore

  mu(H_i)M+mu(H_j)M >= V_i+V_j+vol_d(B).

Brunn-Minkowski gives the displayed lower bound on vol_d(B), proving (V).
For equal exclusive volumes V_i=V_j=V, this yields V<=2 tau M/3.

This inequality uses full convex fiber geometry and the integer midpoint;
it is stronger than the pointwise incidence condition (P). It does not yet
control how volume promotions from many pairs overlap at the same fibers.

## Same-fiber witness consequences

At most d+1 certificate witnesses can have exactly the same integer
coordinate. Otherwise Radon's theorem partitions d+2 such continuous
points into disjoint groups with intersecting convex hulls. Their common
point lies in S_plus and strictly outside every cap: for a cap represented
in one group, use the opposite group; for other caps use either group.
This contradicts the open cover.

For any two distinct witnesses in the same fiber, the corresponding caps
also overlap there in positive d-volume. Choose small positive-volume balls
in their respective exclusive regions. Their convex hull lies outside all
other caps and is covered by the two open caps. A segment between interior
points of the balls starts exclusively in one cap and ends exclusively in
the other. Connectedness forces a point in both open caps, and that point
lies in the interior of the convex hull; hence the overlap has positive
volume.

Neither statement applies merely from equality of parity. In particular,
a bound of d+1 witnesses per parity class requires an additional argument;
the pointwise condition (P) does not provide it.

## Finite-family volume promotion with fiberwise overlap controlled

Choose any nonempty set I of certificate indices, and compact convex
positive-volume exclusive pieces A_i in the witness fibers, i in I.
Write V_i=vol_d(A_i), Q=conv{z_i:i in I}, and for z in Q define

  f_I(z)=max {sum_{i in I} lambda_i V_i^(1/d):
              lambda_i>=0, sum lambda_i=1,
              sum lambda_i z_i=z}.

The maximum exists because the feasible set is a nonempty compact polytope.
Then the following exact bound holds:

  |I| tau M >= sum_{z in Q intersect Z^n}
       max{ f_I(z)^d, sum_{i in I:z_i=z} V_i }.       (FVP)

Proof. A maximizing set of coefficients at z defines the Minkowski sum
A(lambda)=sum lambda_i A_i. It lies in C_z and strictly outside every cap
whose index is not in I. Hence the open cover puts the whole Minkowski sum
inside the union of the caps indexed by I. Repeated Brunn-Minkowski gives
vol_d(A(lambda))>=f_I(z)^d. In addition, all exclusive pieces with integer
coordinate z lie in this union and are pairwise disjoint, so its z-fiber
has volume at least their summed volumes. Summing the larger of these two
lower bounds over integer fibers proves a lower bound for the mass of the
union of caps in I. The union's mass is at most the sum |I| tau M. QED.

For example, if k distinct witness coordinates have the same parity and
all their chosen exclusive pieces have equal volume V, then f_I is the
constant V^(1/d) on Q. The set Q intersect Z^n contains all pairwise
midpoints of the k coordinates and therefore at least 2k-1 points. To see
the count directly, order the coordinates by a generic linear functional;
the k sums of the smallest with each point and the k-1 sums of the largest
with every point except the smallest are distinct. Dividing them by two
produces integer points in Q. Consequently

  V <= [k/(2k-1)] tau M.

This family version counts each newly forced integer fiber once and thus
avoids unjustified addition of overlapping pairwise volume promotions.
What it does not establish is a lower bound on the exclusive volumes V_i
in terms of tau or the total mass. Such a bound is needed before (FVP) can
contradict the hypothesized sharp small-cap cover.

## Exact mixed Brunn-Minkowski inequality via monotone fiber coupling

Let d>=1. Let A,B be compact subsets of Z^n x R^d with positive finite
mixed volumes a=vol_MI(A), b=vol_MI(B). Then

  vol_MI(A+B)^(1/d) >= a^(1/d)+b^(1/d).             (MBM)

If A and B lie in the same parity class (p+2Z^n) x R^d, their midpoint
set lies in the mixed lattice, and consequently

  vol_MI((A+B)/2)
     >= ((a^(1/d)+b^(1/d))/2)^d.                   (PMBM)

No convexity of A or B, nor sampled log-concavity, is assumed here. The
compactness assumption can be weakened, but suffices for cap applications.

Proof. Ignore zero-volume fibers. List A's integer fiber coordinates
z_1,...,z_k and B's coordinates w_1,...,w_l in increasing order of a generic
linear functional L that is injective separately on these two finite sets.
Write a_i=vol_d(A_{z_i}) and b_j=vol_d(B_{w_j}). Partition [0,1] into
successive intervals of lengths a_i/a and, separately, into successive
intervals of lengths b_j/b. Let q_ij be the length of the intersection of
the corresponding intervals. Then

  q_ij>=0, sum_ij q_ij=1,
  q_ij<=a_i/a, and q_ij<=b_j/b.

The pairs with q_ij>0 form a monotone chain: as their intersection intervals
are traversed from left to right, neither index decreases and at least one
increases. Thus their coordinates z_i+w_j are all distinct, because their
L-values strictly increase.

For each positive q_ij, the fiber of A+B at z_i+w_j contains
A_{z_i}+B_{w_j}. Ordinary d-dimensional Brunn-Minkowski gives its volume at
least (a_i^(1/d)+b_j^(1/d))^d. The bounds on q_ij imply

  (a_i^(1/d)+b_j^(1/d))^d
     >= q_ij (a^(1/d)+b^(1/d))^d.

Because the selected sum coordinates are distinct, these lower bounds may
be added without double counting. Summing q_ij=1 proves (MBM). For the
midpoint version, all selected midpoint coordinates are integers under the
parity hypothesis, and scaling the continuous fiber coordinates by 1/2
multiplies their volumes by 2^{-d}. This proves (PMBM). QED.

The same monotone-quantile proof works for a finite weighted Minkowski sum:
if lambda_s>0 sum to one, A_s have positive volumes a_s, and every output
integer-coordinate combination sum_s lambda_s z_s is an integer, then

  vol_MI(sum_s lambda_s A_s)
       >= (sum_s lambda_s a_s^(1/d))^d.

A sufficient arithmetic condition is that all A_s use the same residue
class modulo an integer m and every m lambda_s is an integer. Intersect all
normalized cumulative fiber-mass partitions of [0,1]; their positive cells
again give a monotone chain of distinct output coordinates. On each cell
q, every participating fiber volume is at least q a_s, and repeated
Brunn-Minkowski proves the bound after summing q.

For d=0, the separate elementary conclusion is |A+B|>=max{|A|,|B|}; an
injection is obtained by translating the larger set by any point of the
other. No undefined 1/d or gamma_0 convention is needed.

The exponent in (PMBM) is exactly d, not n+d. Thickening integer fibers by
unit cubes and applying ambient Brunn-Minkowski would prove a weaker
n+d-exponent inequality; the monotone quantile coupling removes that loss.
Nevertheless, (PMBM) cannot be applied to different parity classes: their
midpoint need not lie in the mixed lattice. This arithmetic restriction is
explicit and remains essential to any application to the small-cap cover.
